title: The article reports 5,011 completed surveys and the deposited data hold fewer respondents
published:
We surveyed 5,011 Americans between June 22 and 27, 2023, using SurveyMonkey's "river sample," wherein a random sample of the platform's over two million daily respondents to customer-generated surveys are invited to take an additional, voluntary survey.

Of the 6,877 respondents that began the survey, [[5,011]] completed it (73 percent).
note: The deposited file, data.csv, holds 4,838 rows, with ids running from 1 to 4,838 and no gaps, and neither the deposit's README.txt nor its codebook mentions an exclusion, so 173 of the respondents the article counts are not in it. Tables 2, A.2, and A.3 reproduce cell for cell from the 4,838 rows, and the three group sizes in Figure 1's caption (see entry 3) are the deposit's own party identification counts exactly, so the analysis sample is the deposited one. The shortfall shows only in Table A.1, a profile of the sample and not an estimate from it: 35 of its 38 cells differ from the published figure, by 0.3 of a point at the median and by no more than 1.4. The weighted Biden approval the article quotes at 40.4 percent comes out at 41.4 percent on the deposited rows. Nothing here establishes that 5,011 is the wrong figure: respondents who began and did not finish are not in any respondent file, so the 173 are absent from the file without that being evidence about the survey. The article's sentence is therefore reprinted as published, and what a reader needs to know is that the deposit cannot rebuild the sample the article describes. No conclusion of the paper changes: Tables 2, A.2, and A.3 reproduce from the deposit as printed, and the article's estimates rest on them.

title: Appendix B calls Table A.2 a numerical version of Figure 1 and the two differ
published: [[Table A2 is a numerical version of figure 1.]]
note: Figure 1 plots unweighted shares of respondents, and Table A.2 reports weighted percentages, so the table's change-format rows do not reproduce the figure's plotted shares. The largest of the 18 disagreements is 3.6 points, in the beliefs block's positive-effect row for the Democratic column: the figure plots 79.5 per cent and the table prints 76.0. Neither number is wrong, since each is the right value for its own weighting, and the repair would be a different sentence about how the two are related, which is the authors' to write.
